newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian concerned by "sophisticated" boat people.
newsitem.headline: Australian concerned by "sophisticated" boat people.

text.p: Australia expressed concern on Monday that the latest arrival of boat people seeking asylum might be part of a sophisticated commercial immigration racket.
The government launched an investigation on Sunday after 139 Asian boat people headed for the east coast of Australia were detained in waters off the nothern tip of the country on Friday.
Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock said the operation, using a modern, well-equipped boat, differed from previous arrivals in old, often unseaworthy vessels.

"My principle concern is that an arrangement of this sort is not put together without a great deal of expense being incurred and nobody incurs that sort of expense without expecting to recoup it," Ruddock said in a radio interview.
"And that would suggest that it's organised and organised in quite a sophisticated way.

"There are new factors that are involved in this (case) -- the size of the venture would be one, the fact that they were using a steel-hulled vessel, the fact that it had quite sophisticated navigaitional equipment were all matters that were quite different ... to those that we've experienced before."
Ruddock would not say where the latest boat people had come from or what language they spoke.
Each year, several hundred illegal immigrants land along the northern coast of this vast but sparsely populated country, or on islands that dot the northern waters.
Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said on Sunday Canberra would take a tougher line against boat people trying to jump immigration queues.
"We are going to be a whole lot more rigorous and maintain that degree of rigour with regard to protecting our borders and maintaining our sovereignty," he said.
"People ought to be aware of that and let that message ripple up the bamboo grapevine so that people can desist from this dangerous and foolhardy queue-jumping."
Australia is a popular destination for immigrants, but sets increasingly tough conditions for applicants.
The immigration intake has been limited to 68,000 in the fiscal year from July, down from 74,000 in 1996/97. Canberra set aside 12,000 places for asylum-seekers in both years.
Ruddock said that despite the concerns over the latest arrivals, the government was not prejudging their asylum bids.
"We go through and test every claim that is made against our international obligations and we obviously don't prejudge those matters before we've dealt with them," he said.
All but two of the latest arrivals were being held at the remote Port Hedland detention centre on the northwest coast.
